prompt: Order these moments in Mexican history from earliest to latest

items.text: Fall of Tenochtitlan to Cortés and allies
Battle of Puebla (the original Cinco de Mayo)
Madero's call to revolt starts the Mexican Revolution

explanation: Nearly six centuries in five steps: an island city, a conquest, a shout for independence, a surprise win over France, then a revolution.

source.title: Gob.mx / Memórica: fundación de México-Tenochtitlan
source.verification: Gob.mx page says historians agree the founding was in 1325. Ciencia UNAM (ciencia.unam.mx/leer/1102) dates the fall with Cuauhtémoc's capture on 13 Aug 1521. gob.mx/defensa document dates the Grito to the early hours of 16 Sep 1810. INAH Museo del Caracol (lugares.inah.gob.mx/en/node/4240) and bicentenariobc.gob.mx chronology describe Zaragoza's 1862 victory at Puebla. Library of Congress timeline (loc.gov/exhibits/mexican-revolution-and-the-united-states/timeline.html) says Madero's Plan of San Luis Potosí called for an uprising on 20 Nov 1910. Checked 2026-10-27.

prompt: Order these Mexico City landmarks by the year they were completed or inaugurated
explanation: The cathedral took about 240 years to finish, so it wins 'earliest' despite starting in the 1500s; the museum went up in a brisk 19 months.

source.title: INAH Catálogo Nacional de Monumentos Históricos: Conjunto Catedral Metropolitana
source.verification: INAH catalogue: cathedral construction began 1573 and was concluded 1813. Secretaría de Cultura / gob.mx (gob.mx/cultura/prensa/la-columna-de-la-independencia-...) : Columna de la Independencia inaugurated by Porfirio Díaz 16 Sep 1910. INBA (inba.gob.mx/prensa/22803) : Palacio de Bellas Artes inaugurated 29 Sep 1934. CDMX tourism (mexicocity.cdmx.gob.mx/venues/torre-latinoamericana) : construction 1948 to 1956, tallest in the city from 1956. Chapultepec/Cultura and INAH (mna.inah.gob.mx) : museum inaugurated 17 Sep 1964, built in 19 months. Checked 2026-10-27.

prompt: Order these Mexican traditions by the year UNESCO inscribed them as Intangible Cultural Heritage

items.text: Indigenous festivity dedicated to the dead (Día de Muertos)
Talavera ceramics of Puebla and Tlaxcala

explanation: The ofrenda got listed first; the serenades, cowboys, pottery and love songs followed. (Día de Muertos was proclaimed a Masterpiece in 2003, then moved onto the list in 2008.)

source.title: UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage: Mexico, elements on the lists
source.verification: UNESCO ICH page lists: Indigenous festivity dedicated to the dead 2008; Mariachi 2011; Charrería 2016; Talavera (shared with Spain) 2019; Bolero (shared) 2023. sic.cultura.gob.mx notes the 2003 Masterpiece proclamation preceding the 2008 inscription. Checked 2026-10-27.

Checked 2026-10-27.

prompt: Order these Mexican Revolution events from earliest to latest

items.text: Díaz tells a US magazine Mexico is ready for democracy
Villa and Orozco capture Ciudad Juárez
Pancho Villa raids Columbus, New Mexico
Obregón sworn in, ending the Revolution

explanation: One magazine interview in 1908 helped kick off twelve years of upheaval.

source.title: Library of Congress: The Mexican Revolution and the United States, timeline
source.verification: LOC timeline: Creelman interview with Díaz published March 1908; Orozco and Villa take Ciudad Juárez 10 May 1911; Villa raids Columbus NM 9 Mar 1916; Obregón sworn in 30 Nov 1920, Revolution over. Checked 2026-10-27.
